how-much-to-charge-for-dog-boarding.html.text:
← Dog boarding & daycare pricing calculator

How much to charge for dog boarding

Search this question and you get a range: twenty-five to seventy-five dollars a night, more for large dogs or cities. The range is not wrong, and it is not usable, because it hides the four things that actually decide whether a night pays: staff time, supplies, overhead, and the margin you need to keep running.

Open the free boarding & daycare calculator

What one night actually costs to deliver

Thirty minutes of staff time — feeding, potty breaks, play, cleaning the run — at an $18/hour wage is $9.00. Add $4.00 of food, bedding, and cleaning supplies, and a $10.00 share of rent, utilities, and insurance allocated to that one dog-day, and the true cost to deliver one night is $23.00 before you have kept a dollar.

LineAmount
Staff labor (0.5 hr × $18/hr)$9.00
Supplies$4.00
Overhead allocated$10.00
Cost to deliver$23.00
Margin (25%)$5.75
Price per night$28.75
3-night reservation$86.25

That $28.75 is not a market rate and does not have to match what any other facility charges — it is what your own staff time, supplies, and overhead actually require. Raise the wage, the overhead share, or the margin, and the number moves; that is the calculator working as intended, not a flaw in it.

Why a second dog isn't a second full price

A second dog from the same family shares the run, the feeding trip, and most of the potty-break time the first dog already accounts for. Charging a full second stay overprices the easiest booking a facility gets — the one that needs no second kennel and no second cleaning cycle.

Two dogs for three nights at a 10% multi-dog discount is $163.88, not $172.50. The $8.63 discount reflects the real extra cost of a second dog far better than doubling the price does, and it is often the difference between keeping a multi-dog family's business and losing it to a facility that already discounts.

The long-stay discount trap

A long stay is worth discounting — it fills a run for one booking instead of several, and it competes with the weekly rate other facilities already advertise. But discounting the whole stay gives away margin on nights that cost exactly the same to deliver as a short booking. The fix is a threshold: discount only the nights beyond it.

NightsAt full rateAt discountDiscountTotal
10 (threshold 7, 10% off past it)7 × $28.753 × $25.88$8.63$278.88

A flat 10% off the whole 10-night stay would have priced it at $258.75 — $20.13 less than the threshold-based discount recovers, for exactly the same booking. The nights every stay has in common should not subsidize the discount meant to win the long ones.

What a nightly rate can't tell you: occupancy

Pricing one reservation well is half the question. The other half is whether the facility as a whole is profitable, which depends on how many of its runs are actually filled across a month — not on any single stay's price.

FigureValue
Kennel/run count12
Monthly dog-day capacity (12 runs × 30 days)360
Fixed monthly costs$6,000.00
Average realized rate$45.00
Variable cost per dog-day$13.00
Break-even occupancy52.1% (187.5 dog-days)

At a projected 65% occupancy (234.0 dog-days), the facility clears break-even and nets a $1,488.00 monthly profit. At 30% occupancy (108.0 dog-days) with the same rate, it falls 22.1 points short of break-even and loses $2,544.00 for the month. Two very different months, one nightly rate — occupancy is the variable a per-stay price alone cannot see.

Common questions

How much should I charge for dog boarding per night?

There is no single right answer, because a nightly rate hides four separate costs: staff time, supplies, facility overhead, and the margin you need to keep. A worked example with 30 minutes of staff time at an $18/hour wage, $4 of supplies, and $10 of allocated overhead costs $23.00 per dog-day to deliver, and prices at $28.75/night with a 25 percent margin. Your own numbers will differ, and that is the point: the rate has to come from your costs, not from what a competitor posts.

Should a second dog from the same family cost twice as much?

No, and pricing it that way loses multi-dog bookings. A second dog in the same reservation adds handling effort but not a second kennel run, a second cleaning cycle, or a second staff trip, so charging a full second stay overprices the easiest booking a facility gets. A 10 percent multi-dog discount on the example above turns two dogs for three nights into $163.88 instead of $172.50 -- an $8.63 discount that keeps the family's business without giving away margin on the parts of the stay that really did double.

Why discount long stays, and why only past a threshold?

A long stay is worth discounting because it fills a calendar for one booking instead of several, and it competes with weekly rates other facilities already offer. But the first several nights of any stay cost exactly the same to deliver as a short one, so discounting the whole stay gives away margin you never needed to. In the worked example, a 10-night stay bills the first 7 nights at the full $28.75 rate and only the remaining 3 at a 10 percent discount -- $8.63 off a $287.50 flat total, landing at $278.88.

Why isn't a nightly rate enough to know if my facility is profitable?

Because a nightly rate prices one dog for one night, and a facility's profit depends on how many of its runs are actually filled across a whole month. A 12-run facility with $6,000 in fixed monthly costs and a $45 average realized rate needs 52.1 percent occupancy just to break even -- roughly 187.5 of its 360 monthly dog-day slots. At a more realistic 65 percent occupancy it clears that with room to spare, turning a $1,488.00 monthly profit; at 30 percent it falls 22.1 points short of break-even and loses $2,544.00 for the month at the same rate. The rate alone cannot tell you which of those two months you are having.

Does this replace pricing software or a booking platform?

No. This tool has no booking, no calendar, no payment processing, and no client messaging -- it only prices a reservation and checks occupancy math. Plenty of facilities run a booking or kennel-management platform for scheduling and use a separate calculation, like this one, to decide what to actually charge.

Run it on your own facility

The calculator prices one reservation from your own staff time, supplies, overhead, and discounts, and checks whether your kennel/run occupancy clears a monthly break-even. It runs entirely in your browser.

Open the free boarding & daycare calculator

Weighing this against just matching a competitor's posted rate? See this calculator vs. a flat nightly rate.

Common questions

Why does a second dog on the same reservation cost less than doubling the price?

Because almost none of the per-dog-day cost doubles with a second dog from the same household. The run, the feeding routine, and most of the potty-break time are already happening — a second dog adds handling effort but not a second kennel, a second cleaning cycle, or a second staff trip. Pricing it as a full second stay is the fastest way to lose a multi-dog family to a competitor who discounts it.

Why does the long-stay discount only apply past a threshold, not to the whole stay?

Because the first several nights of any stay cost the same to deliver as a short booking — there is no efficiency gained yet. The discount exists to win multi-week bookings that would otherwise go to a competitor's weekly rate, and applying it only to the nights beyond the threshold protects margin on the nights every stay has in common, short or long.

Why does the calculator separate a per-stay overhead assumption from the facility's fixed monthly costs?

They answer different questions. The per-reservation price needs a quick per-dog-day overhead estimate to fold into a quote. The occupancy section needs the facility's actual fixed costs (rent, utilities, insurance, software) and kennel/run count to find the occupancy percentage that breaks even — a number that a per-stay estimate alone cannot produce, because break-even depends on how many of your runs are actually filled, not on any one reservation's price.

Does anything about my facility or reservations get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server and there is no account. Your reservation and facility inputs are saved locally on this device so you don't retype them — Reset to defaults clears them, and Copy shareable link puts them in a URL fragment your browser never sends anywhere. vs-a-flat-nightly-rate.html.text:
← Dog boarding & daycare pricing calculator

This calculator vs. a flat nightly rate

The fastest way to price a dog boarding stay is to see what other local facilities charge and pick a similar number. It is also the most common way, and it names no product or company this page could be affiliated with -- it is a habit every independent facility owner already has, not a piece of software. This page compares that habit to using this calculator's cost-and-occupancy model instead.

A flat rate copied from a competitor answers one question: what does the market seem to tolerate? It cannot answer a different one, which is the one that actually decides whether the business works: does this rate cover what a stay of mine actually costs, and does my own occupancy at that rate add up to a month that pays?

QuestionFlat competitor rateThis calculator
What does the market seem to tolerate? Answers it directly. Does not know your competitors' rates at all.
Does the rate cover my own staff time, supplies, and overhead? No way to check -- it is one number with no arithmetic behind it. Builds the rate from your own cost inputs, so the answer is always yes by construction.
Is a second dog on the same reservation priced right? Usually just doubled, or discounted by feel. A named multi-dog discount percentage, applied consistently.
Should a long stay be discounted, and by how much? Often a flat percentage off the whole stay, which gives away margin on nights that cost the same as a short booking. A threshold-based discount: full rate up to a set night count, discount only beyond it.
Does my facility's occupancy at this rate actually break even? Not answered by a nightly rate at all -- that is a whole-facility, whole-month question. Computes the break-even occupancy percentage and profit or shortfall at a projected occupancy.
Price your own reservation and occupancy

This tool needs no account and names no competitor: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your reservation and facility numbers stay on your device -- nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

What is wrong with just picking a flat nightly rate?

Nothing is wrong with landing on one number to quote -- that is what every facility does in the end. What a flat rate picked by matching a competitor's posted price does not do is tell you whether that number covers your own staff time, supplies, and overhead, whether a second dog on the same reservation is priced right, whether a long stay should be discounted and by how much without giving away margin on the nights every stay has in common, or whether your facility's occupancy at that rate actually breaks even in a real month. A flat rate is an answer with no arithmetic behind it; this calculator supplies the arithmetic and lets you land on whatever number you want afterward.

Isn't matching what other local facilities charge a reasonable way to set a rate?

It tells you what the market will tolerate, which is real information -- but it says nothing about whether that rate covers your specific costs. Two facilities charging the same $35 a night can have completely different margins if one pays more per hour for staff, carries higher rent, or runs at a lower occupancy. Matching a competitor's rate without checking it against your own cost stack and occupancy is how a facility ends up busy and unprofitable at the same time.

Does this calculator tell me what to actually charge?

No, and it is not trying to. It has no data on what any other facility charges, does not recommend a market rate, and does not know your local competition. It takes the costs and assumptions you supply -- staff time, wage, supplies, overhead, discounts, occupancy -- and does the arithmetic honestly. The rate you land on, and whether it beats or matches a competitor, is your decision.

Why does occupancy matter if my nightly rate already covers my costs?

Because a per-stay price only covers the cost of the dogs you actually have. Fixed costs -- rent, utilities, insurance, software -- keep accruing whether a run is filled or empty, so a rate that comfortably covers cost per dog-day can still leave the facility unprofitable for the month if too many runs sit empty. A flat nightly rate answers "is this one stay priced right?"; it cannot answer "is this month going to work?", which is a question about occupancy across the whole facility, not about any one reservation.
